A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PiCa by the same authors and retain its central method, Theorem 1, and NLP experiments. All pages, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original PiCa benchmark results, weight-sharing ablations, memory measurements, and analyses of fine-tuned weights. Attribution of baseline scores to SVFT does not change the originality of the PiCa results.

after.justification: V2 retains original PiCa NLP results and adds vision experiments, a projection-choice ablation, and LLaMA3-8B spectral analysis.

M1.justification: Both versions use fixed top-r left singular vectors of pretrained weights and a zero-initialized compact matrix shared across layers with the same functional role. V2 Algorithm 1 documents gradient aggregation and compact Adam updates, renaming B to theta; it does not establish a changed adaptation procedure.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and natural language understanding. V2 retains this coverage and adds visual adaptation on 19 VTAB-1K datasets and subject-driven image generation on DreamBooth (Section 4 and Table 4), substantially extending the evaluated domains and tasks.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained NLP tables is unchanged. V2 Table 5 adds a random-space projection control, while the vision experiments reuse LoRA, DoRA, VeRA, and SVFT. V1's separate SVFT memory comparison and Full FT/LoRA learning-behavior comparisons are removed.

E3.justification: New protocols evaluate ViT-B/16 with ten training epochs and best-validation checkpoint selection, and Stable Diffusion v2.1 with 30 subjects, 25 prompts per subject, and DINO/CLIP-T metrics. Appendix C.3 adds layer-aggregated Diagonal Similarity measurements on LLaMA3-8B. Settings for retained NLP experiments, including hyperparameter Tables 6–8, are unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a matched-budget column-versus-random projection ablation and a larger-model test of spectral-stability assumptions (Table 5 and Appendix C.3). It removes v1's memory profiling, spectral-similarity heatmaps, and magnitude/direction analysis (Table 5 and Figures 1 and 5). The perturbation histogram and weight-sharing/rank studies are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Table 10 introduces plus/minus summaries for similarity and perturbation statistics aggregated across layers. Neither version reports training seed or repeated-run counts, and v2 does not define the reported spread. This changes statistical reporting without establishing additional training runs; benchmark performance uncertainty remains unreported.

E6.justification: The retained NLP scores are unchanged. New results include PiCa's VTAB overall score of 0.697, DreamBooth DINO/CLIP-T scores of 0.634/0.306, random-projection accuracy of 63.18 versus column projection's 67.60, and LLaMA3-8B spectral statistics. V1's memory measurements—16.73 GB for PiCa versus 20.23/20.68 GB for SVFT—and learning-behavior results are removed.

T1.justification: V2 adds a Wedin-style subspace perturbation lemma, an L-smoothness definition, and Theorem 2 bounding sequential versus accumulated gradient projection under smoothness and bounded-gradient assumptions, with a new Appendix B proof. It also adds the non-expansiveness lemma for orthogonal projection. Theorem 1 and its essential derivation are retained.

C1.justification: V2 broadens the headline contribution from LLM/NLP adaptation to foundation-model adaptation across NLP and vision, emphasizing a theoretical justification for sequential gradient projection. V1's explicit priority claim, closer-to-Full-FT learning claim, and quantified SVFT memory advantage disappear from the central contributions. The main parameter-efficiency claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 motivates stable singular subspaces through small fine-tuning updates and regularization, and interprets the random-projection control as evidence for the value of pretrained geometry. It removes v1's explanations of SVFT memory overhead and PiCa's Full-FT-like magnitude/direction behavior. Both versions retain the SVD loading-cost versus adapter-storage tradeoff in Section 5.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 newly specifies gradient aggregation, compact Adam moment states, bias correction, and reconstruction of layer updates. Appendix C.1 adds vision adaptation targets, method-specific learning rates, classifier learning rate, and checkpoint selection. These substantially expand implementation documentation; retained NLP hyperparameters and code/data access instructions are unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 removes the PiSSA discussion and adds SVDiff and DiTASK as important spectral-adaptation precedents. Punica newly motivates multi-adapter deployment, while vision and Wedin references support the expanded scope. Positioning shifts from LoRA-versus-Full-FT behavior and SVFT memory costs toward theoretical justification of geometry-based adaptation.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively revised. Section 3 is reorganized around subspace projection, sequential gradients, and the algorithm; Appendix B's numbered proof steps become a continuous derivation. V2 adds Appendices C.3, D, and E, and renames the retained Natural Language Generation experiments Mathematical Reasoning.

P2.justification: V2 adds Algorithm 1 and Tables 4, 5, and 10, while removing v1's gradient-comparison and memory tables and Figures 1 and 5. The retained accuracy plot, perturbation histogram, and sharing plots are relocated and renumbered. The document also adopts different title/header styling and extensively reflows and resizes displays.

improvement.justification: V2's matched-budget projection control directly tests a central design choice left untested in v1, and its vision experiments provide useful evidence beyond NLP. Algorithm 1 improves implementation clarity, while Theorem 2 supplies a conditional argument for gradient descent. These gains are partly offset by removing measured memory costs and Full-FT behavior diagnostics; the new theorem also does not directly analyze shared Adam training. The net improvement is useful but limited.
